content.text:
What makes galaxies and black holes so fascinating?

A galaxy holding hundreds of billions of stars and a black hole that not even light can escape are the most mysterious things in the universe. They stretch a child's imagination all the way to the edge of space.

content.alt: Galaxies and Black Holes - Nature and science facts about galaxies and black holes
content.text:
Nature and science facts about galaxies and black holes

A galaxy is a huge collection of tens to hundreds of billions of stars and gas bound together by gravity. There are about 2 trillion galaxies in the universe, and our galaxy (the Milky Way) is a barred spiral galaxy. A black hole is an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape; it forms when a giant star reaches the end of its life, explodes, and its core is compressed.

content.alt: Galaxies and Black Holes - How to explore the universe more deeply
content.text:
How to explore the universe more deeply

Point out things like the galaxy (a home for stars), our galaxy (the Milky Way), the black hole (even light can't escape), and the kinds of galaxies (spiral and elliptical). Try imagining together, "What would happen if you went into a black hole?"

content.alt: Galaxies and Black Holes - Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on play
content.text:
Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on play

In a dark room, look at photos and videos of the Milky Way together and draw a swirl (a spiral galaxy). For a black hole, comparing it to "a vacuum cleaner that even sucks in light" helps a child understand it easily.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What is a galaxy?
A. It's a huge collection of tens to hundreds of billions of stars and gas bound together by gravity. Our galaxy is the Milky Way.

Q. What is a black hole?
A. It's an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. It forms at the very end of a giant star's life.

Q. How can we enjoy it at home?
A. Look at Milky Way photos, draw spirals, and imagine a black hole as a "light vacuum cleaner."
